frameworks.name: Upside-Downside-Livability Filter
frameworks.definition: A three-question decision filter (What is the upside? What is the downside? Can I live with the downside?) attributed by Alex Hormozi to Keith Cunningham, used to evaluate strategic pivots and major bets.

frameworks.name: Licensing Readiness Gate
frameworks.definition: Alex Hormozi's conditional approval framework: a founder earns the right to launch a licensing model only after the business can open a new location per quarter with a team that does not include the founder at all.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that franchising is a poor capital structure for low-margin businesses because a franchise transfers almost all of the business's value to the franchisee in exchange for a royalty, making it the most expensive form of capital available. In a business earning roughly 15% net margin on $500K per-location revenue (approximately $75K net per location), a licensing fee of 6-8% of top-line revenue captures nearly as much cash as the owner's current net profit while preserving cross-state expansion without the capital commitment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business net margin approximately 15% or lower
Per-location revenue approximately $500K
Owner not willing to give away operating control
claims.mechanism: At 15% net margin, franchising transfers nearly all operating value to the franchisee while the owner retains only a royalty; licensing at 6-8% of top-line captures comparable economics while preserving ownership and cross-state flexibility.

numbers.axis: owner cash capture per location at $500K revenue

bounded_by: Does not apply when net margins are high enough that franchising royalties are a small fraction of profit
Does not apply when the primary goal is rapid capital deployment rather than cross-state expansion

claims.text: Alex Hormozi advises that a founder should not pursue a licensing or expansion model until the core business can open new locations at a rate of at least one per quarter using a team that does not involve the founder. Once that capability exists, the founder will likely no longer feel urgency to launch the licensing model because the core business growth becomes satisfying on its own.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business with geographic expansion potential
Founder currently involved in opening new locations
claims.mechanism: If a founder must be personally involved in each new location opening, the licensing model will face the same founder-bottleneck problem at greater complexity; solving location-opening systemization first removes that constraint and often dissolves the urgency to license.

numbers.axis: location-opening cadence as licensing readiness gate

anchors.value: founder required for each new location opening
one new location per quarter opened by team without founder

bounded_by: Specific to founder-involved service businesses; does not apply to software or fully automated models

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that in a fixed-reimbursement insurance-based service business where price cannot be raised, improving net margin by 10 percentage points (e.g., from 15% to 25% on $500K per-location revenue) produces an approximately 67% improvement in bottom-line profit per location — equivalent in cash terms to opening six additional locations, which could realistically be achieved in roughly six months.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Insurance-reimbursed service business where price is set externally
Current net margin approximately 15%
Per-location revenue approximately $500K
claims.mechanism: Because price is fixed by insurance reimbursement schedules, the only controllable lever is cost of goods and operational efficiency; each percentage point of margin improvement therefore multiplies directly into bottom-line cash at the same rate as opening equivalent new revenue.

numbers.axis: net profit improvement from margin gain vs. new location equivalent

anchors.region: after 10pp margin improvement (25% net margin on $500K)

anchors.value: ~6 locations to generate the same incremental $50K net

bounded_by: Only applies when top-line price is externally fixed (e.g., insurance rate schedules); does not apply when price is a controllable lever

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that VC-funded competitors in a category who have raised significant capital and deployed smart teams but have not achieved profitability should be treated as evidence that the path they are pursuing is genuinely difficult, not as evidence that the incumbent profitable business should pivot to match them.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Incumbent has a profitable, slower-growing model
Well-funded competitors exist but have not achieved profitability
claims.mechanism: If well-capitalized teams with talented people cannot make a model profitable, the prior probability that an undercapitalized founder can do so is low; abandoning a working profitable model for an unproven one transfers certain upside for uncertain downside.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the VC model is in a regulated window that will open; does not apply when incumbents have strong evidence their cost structure is fundamentally different

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that at sufficient revenue scale (roughly $40M annual revenue), the organizational structure of any service business converges to the same ~7-10 functional heads (sales, marketing, product/CS, IT, legal, finance, AR/AP), making the specific industry or service type largely irrelevant to the founder's daily experience of running the company.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business has reached sufficient scale to require full functional management team
claims.mechanism: At scale, a founder's daily work becomes managing 7-10 senior leaders regardless of industry; industry-specific complexity is absorbed into those functional roles, so the founder's lived experience is equivalent across widgets, wellness, or motorcycles.

numbers.axis: functional heads required by revenue level

anchors.value: 7-10 functional heads (sales, marketing, product/CS, IT, legal, finance, AR/AP)

bounded_by: Does not apply to purely software businesses where functional structures differ
Does not apply to solo-operator lifestyle businesses that never reach functional-head scale

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends that before pursuing a new strategic model (licensing, franchising, virtual pivot), a business owner apply Keith Cunningham's three-question filter: (1) What is the upside? (2) What is the downside? (3) Can I live with the downside? A fourth optional question is: How likely is the downside? If the downside is unlivable regardless of its probability, the action should not be taken.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder evaluating a major strategic pivot or capital-intensive expansion
Current business is profitable and growing
claims.mechanism: Explicit downside enumeration prevents founders from being seduced by upside framing while suppressing awareness of asymmetric loss scenarios; the liveability test forces a binary check that bypasses optimism bias.
bounded_by: The filter is a decision gate, not a strategic optimization — it does not generate new options, only eliminates ones with unacceptable downside

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that when a wellness or health service business has fixed insurance reimbursement rates (approximately $150/hour for dietitian services) and must pay dietitians, admin, and marketing from that fixed rate, the resulting net margins are structurally thin, making VC-backed virtual-only operators economically fragile even at high volume.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Insurance-reimbursed healthcare service business
Reimbursement rate approximately $150/hour
Labor-intensive delivery model (dietitians, admin, marketing)
claims.mechanism: A fixed reimbursement ceiling combined with non-compressible labor costs (clinician, admin, marketing) produces structurally thin margins; scaling volume does not improve margins in this model because each additional unit of revenue requires proportional labor cost.

numbers.axis: cost layers within $150/hour insurance reimbursement for dietitian service

bounded_by: Does not apply to supplement sales, coaching, or other non-insurance revenue streams with controllable pricing

claims.text: Alex Hormozi observes that a founder who spreads focus across adjacent opportunities (gym alongside dietitian clinic, licensing model, training university for dietitians) consistently underperforms a founder who focuses exclusively on the proven core vehicle, because team capacity and founder attention are finite and dilute proportionally across parallel initiatives.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder leading a sub-$10M service business
Multiple adjacent opportunities visible simultaneously
claims.mechanism: Each additional initiative claims a proportional share of founder attention and team bandwidth; because execution quality is roughly linear with focused effort, splitting attention across N initiatives produces roughly 1/N execution quality on each, with coordination costs further reducing net output.
bounded_by: Does not apply when a business has a fully autonomous operator layer that can run initiatives independently

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the grass-is-greener cognitive bias causes founders to overestimate the upside of pivoting to an alternative model while underestimating the hidden costs and execution risks, because unfamiliar models have their costs and failure modes invisible to the observer.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder operating a profitable but slower-growing business
A faster-growing alternative model exists with visible success metrics
claims.mechanism: Visible upside of an unfamiliar model is salient; its costs (execution complexity, regulatory burden, margin compression at scale) are invisible until the founder is inside the model. This asymmetric information creates systematic overconfidence in pivots.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the founder has deep inside knowledge of the alternative model from prior experience

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that in a regional service business generating referrals primarily from 18 ancillary practitioners (approximately 400 referrals per month at $3.5M revenue), the existing referral network represents a largely untapped growth lever that should be exhausted before building new acquisition channels.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Referral-dominant acquisition model (>70% of leads from provider network)
Business has not yet systematically scaled or deepened its referral partner relationships

numbers.axis: referral volume per partner base size

bounded_by: Assumes referral partners can absorb additional volume; does not apply if partner network is saturated

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when a business can absorb a capacity doubling (i.e., if referrals doubled tomorrow, nothing would break), it has resolved its supply constraint and is ready to invest in demand generation. The test of operational readiness is not revenue but the capacity to handle a sudden 2x demand spike without breaking core systems.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: if you doubled your referrals tomorrow, what would break?
conditions: Service business seeking to scale demand
Founder unsure whether to invest in marketing or operations first
claims.mechanism: If core systems (front, middle, back office) break at 2x demand, marketing spend multiplies the problem rather than accelerating growth; fixing supply constraints first means every dollar of demand generation returns incremental revenue rather than friction.
bounded_by: The 2x test is a binary gate, not a precision instrument; businesses with deeply seasonal demand may need to test against their own peak rather than a uniform 2x

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that M&A of existing small practices (rather than de novo location openings or licensing) is the fastest path to $10M revenue for a regional wellness group, because an acquired practice already has team, clientele, and physical infrastructure — reducing time-to-productive from approximately 12 months (de novo) to approximately 6 months.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Regional service business with replicable operating system and internal training
Target market has many small sub-$1M practices
Acquirer has 6-month integration playbook
claims.mechanism: A de novo location requires building team, clientele, and operational systems from scratch; an acquired location has those assets in place and requires only systems-replacement, which the acquirer's internal training portal can deliver in roughly 6 months.

numbers.axis: time to productive new location by method

anchors.value: approximately 6 months to adopt acquirer systems

bounded_by: Assumes the acquirer has a documented training system; without that, de novo and acquisition timelines converge
Depends on availability of willing sellers at reasonable valuations

examples.text: The wellness clinic founder described a two-year operational improvement project triggered by Alex Hormozi's question: if referrals doubled tomorrow, what would break? The answer at the time was everything — front office, middle, and back office — all would collapse. The founder spent two years fixing those operational constraints before returning to focus on demand generation. This sequence (fix supply, then scale demand) is offered as evidence that the 2x capacity test is a practical diagnostic for operational readiness.

Alex Hormozi cited his neighbor Mr. Panda, who built a 3.7 billion top-line chicken restaurant business (selling Kung Pao, General Tso's, and similar dishes) over 45 years, one location at a time. Hormozi used this example to argue that a regional wellness clinic reaching $40M over 10 years via organic single-location openings is a legitimate and comparable compounding path, and that the founder's impatience with a 10-year timeline reflects the grass-is-greener bias rather than a genuine strategic problem.

The wellness clinic founder described receiving acquisition offers from two VC-backed virtual-only dietitian groups who wanted to buy the clinic specifically because they could not replicate its quality metrics and client engagement at scale. Hormozi used this anecdote to validate the claim that VC-funded competitors with speed and capital still failed to solve the quality problem, supporting the argument that the incumbent profitable model has durable advantages the well-funded alternatives have not cracked.

The founder described a recurring pattern of adding adjacent ideas — a gym alongside the dietitian clinic because trainers are next door, a licensing model for other dietitians, a case-specific university to train dietitians — each of which seemed logical in isolation but collectively split the founder's time and team across too many parallel initiatives. Hormozi identified this as the core focus problem preventing faster growth of the proven core business.

practices.text: Before pursuing a licensing or franchise model, build and document an internal training system capable of converting an acquired practice to your operating standards in 6 months without founder involvement.

In a fixed-price insurance reimbursement business, audit cost of goods sold and operational workflows for efficiency improvements before investing in new locations or licensing — margin improvement is a faster path to cash than revenue growth.
When evaluating a strategic pivot, explicitly enumerate the downside scenario and ask whether you can live with it before assessing upside probability.
Do not invest in demand generation until the core business can handle a 2x sudden demand spike across front, middle, and back office without breaking.
